## `group` and `mutate` to make sub totals

::: {.incremental}
- The `summarise()` function changes the entire data frame and gives only the statistics
in the function.
- What if you wanted to add it to an existing data frame?
:::

## Total and Percentages by month and org

Let's create new columns with totals and percentages by each period and org_code

Long hand with `dplyr`

```{r}
library(NHSRdatasets)

data <- NHSRdatasets::ae_attendances

data |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    total_attend = sum(attendances),
    perc_attend = (attendances / total_attend) * 100,
    .by = c(org_code, period)
  )
```

## And using the package `janitor`

Using a small subset so we can see the bottom of the data frame

```{r}
data |> 
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 5) |> 
  janitor::adorn_totals(where = "row")


data |> 
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 5) |> 
  janitor::adorn_totals(where = "col",
                        name = "total_attend")

```

## Over to you

The dplyr code can create a pretty long decimal as a percentage

```{r}
data |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    total_attend = sum(attendances),
    perc_attend = (attendances / total_attend) * 100,
    .by = c(org_code, period)
  )
```

Can you round it to 1 decimal place using the function `round()`?

:::{.callout-tip collapse=false appearance='default' icon=true}
- Be very mindful of your commas and brackets!
- There are settings in Tools > Global Options... > Code > Display related to brackets
:::

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(
  minutes = 7,
  color_border = "#005EB8",
  color_text = "#005EB8",
  color_running_text = "white",
  color_running_background = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_text = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_background = "white",
  margin = "0.9em",
  font_size = "2em"
)
```

## Answer - adding `round()` to restrict to 1 decimal place

```{r}
data |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    total_attend = sum(attendances),
    perc_attend = round((attendances / total_attend) * 100, 1),
    .by = c(org_code, period)
  )

```
